supporting_evidence_json: The scope requires graph pages to stay tied to the chosen saved scan and query.
The scope forbids old replies from replacing browser results for a newer choice.
The scope says discovery of every runtime relationship is not guaranteed.
A's page tokens include the saved record version and are refused after a change.
B assumes saved scans never change and keys its cache on scan ID, query fingerprint, view kind and builder version.
B lists its compatibility with parent d734 as unknown.
C keeps a separate loading and error state for each view and claims to work with all three parents.
No source code was supplied. All three alternatives are proposals only.

assessments.change_isolation: A new view kind goes into the same read action. It is simple to start, but changes to different views touch the same code. The design names a later split only when a view needs its own control.
assessments.control_flow: The browser raises its request number and calls the read action. The action checks access, reads the named scan, builds the view and echoes the choice back. The browser checks that echo before changing the screen. Cancelling old work is optional.
assessments.data_ownership: The browser owns the choice, request numbers, pages on screen and loading state. The parent owns saved records and access settings. The server keeps only temporary data for one call.
assessments.decomposition: It has one browser owner of the current choice and display. It has one server read action for all views, paging and history.
assessments.failure_isolation: A failed request changes no saved data. A failed history read gives its own error, and other view requests still work. Late successes and late errors are both thrown away. A storage or application failure still stops all views.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers source structure, relationships, findings and history. It keeps pages tied to the chosen scan and query. Replies are checked so old ones cannot replace newer results. It gives the strongest guard against paging through a record that changes partway.
assessments.justified_complexity: Low. It has two parts and adds no store. The proposal states the missing cache as a known cost, not a hidden one.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs inside the parent application. It needs the parent to give a stable record version, or to refuse paging when a record changes. Its tests cover late replies, reused tokens, refused access and unknown interpretation versions.
strengths: Each page token (a value the browser sends to get the next graph page) records the saved record version. A token is refused if the record changed, so pages from two versions cannot mix.
It says plainly that a page token grants no access. Access is checked again on every request.
It adds no extra service and no stored copy of results, so there is nothing extra to keep up to date.
It refuses to fill gaps in old evidence with today's repository contents.
weaknesses: One server read action builds every view kind and every history comparison. It will grow as view kinds are added.
With no reuse of built views, repeated queries repeat the same expensive reads.
It works with only one parent design (d734). It gives no route to the other two.
It does not say how one browser request number covers views that load at the same time.

assessments.change_isolation: Strong. A new page kind means one new view builder. New query features go into the query evaluator. Raising the builder version keeps old cached pages from being reused.
assessments.control_flow: The browser bumps its counter, updates the URL and sends one request. The handler checks access, then looks in the cache. If the page is not there, it loads the scan, runs the query, builds the page and stores it. It adds the freshness label and echoes the key back. The browser shows the reply only if the key still matches.
assessments.data_ownership: The browser owns the choice and the counter. The parent owns saved scans. The cache owns built pages, which can be thrown away at any time. All other server parts keep nothing between requests.
assessments.decomposition: The browser side has two parts: a selection keeper and a reply check. The server side has a request handler, scan reader, query evaluator, view builders, scan comparer, page cache and freshness label.
assessments.failure_isolation: Late replies are dropped. A missing scan gives a not-found error. A bad query fails before any build starts. A failed build stores nothing. A cache failure only makes pages slower. An unreadable repository only makes freshness show as unknown. A server crash still stops all pages.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers structure, relationships, findings and history. Replies are checked against a key built from the scan, the query, the view kind and a counter. The scope requires pages tied to scan and query, but paging past the first page is not spelled out.
assessments.justified_complexity: Higher than A or C. It has seven server parts and a cache. That is justified only if repeated views are costly. The scope gives no workload numbers, so the cost is not yet shown to be needed.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs in the shared local service. It needs saved scans to keep the same ID and content forever, to carry an input fingerprint, and to mark when they are incomplete. Freshness needs a live fingerprint read of the repository.
strengths: The choice is written into the page address (URL). A reload or a shared link opens the same view.
Each reply names the builder version, the version of the code that made the page. Pages built by older code are then not reused.
History labels each change by its likely cause: different input files, different analysis rules, or uncertain.
The freshness label is added after a page is built and is never stored. So a reused page never shows an old freshness label.
weaknesses: The cache is safe only if saved scans never change. One parent design (d734) does not promise that, and the design admits compatibility with it is unknown.
It has no clear way to ask for the next graph page. It only gives a size limit and a list of what was left out.
The cache has no size limit yet. It can fill up with many query variations.
Its cause labels depend on each scan storing its analysis rules version. The scope does not promise that.
The proposal does not say whether its scan reader reads the parent's storage directly or uses the parent's checked read path.

assessments.change_isolation: Good. History has its own reader. A new view means new request values, result fields and an error state. Parallel paging is put off until measured delays justify it.
assessments.control_flow: A choice change bumps the selection number and starts separate requests for each view. Every reply is checked before it reaches the display. History runs only when the user asks for it. Pages are fetched one at a time per view.
assessments.data_ownership: The selection owner holds choices, numbers and accepted pages. Views hold display details such as graph positions. The parent alone owns saved scans, access settings and freshness checks.
assessments.decomposition: It has a browser selection-and-request owner and a separate display part for views. On the server it has one reader for saved scans and one for history comparisons.
assessments.failure_isolation: Each view fails on its own. When a later graph page fails, the pages already shown stay visible and are marked incomplete. A failed parent read or a server crash still affects every view.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers all four kinds of view. Replies are checked so old ones cannot replace newer results, and continuations cannot change the chosen scan or query. If history records lack version details, it says a difference may come from changed analysis.
assessments.justified_complexity: Moderate. It has four parts and no store. The extra browser bookkeeping pays for itself by keeping views apart when they fail.
assessments.operating_constraints: Readers run in the parent application, and the selection owner runs in the browser. Each parent needs its own route: direct calls, the request gate, or the worker controller. How much browser memory is acceptable is not stated.
strengths: Each view (structure, relationships, findings, history) loads with its own request and keeps its own error state. A history failure does not hide findings that loaded fine.
It keeps two numbers: a selection number and a request number. It gives a new number even when the user goes back to an earlier choice, so an old reply for that same choice is still refused.
It reads only through the parent's allowed, checked read path. It never reads the parent's storage directly.
It claims to work with all three parent designs.
It tells an empty result apart from a failed request.
weaknesses: A page continuation (the value used to fetch the next page) is tied to repository, scan, query and view. It is not tied to a record version. Under a parent whose records can change, pages may mix two versions.
Each separate view request repeats the access and freshness checks.
It allows only one pending page request per view. This makes long graphs slower to load.
Working with three parents means three different ways to send reads, so it has more routing rules to test.

composition_conflicts: B's cache under parent d734: if records can change after saving, the cache could serve pages built from old content. B itself lists this pairing as unknown.
C's continuations under parent d734: they are not tied to a record version, so pages fetched in sequence could mix two record versions.
A works only with parent d734. Pairing it with f0c461 or 877208 is not shown.

B's freshness label reads the live repository's fingerprint. C says the parent alone owns freshness checks. B does go through the parent's check, but its live read must stay within the parent's access rules.
disagreements: Whether saved scans can change: A plans for changes by checking record versions. B depends on scans never changing. C assumes stable IDs but does not check for changes during paging.
Whether reusing built pages is worth it: B adds a cache, while A and C say there is no evidence yet that the cost needs one.
Whether history can explain the cause of a change: B labels causes when a rules version is saved. A and C only show versions that are present and warn when they are missing.

differences: B keeps built pages for reuse, and A and C do not. B's cache is safe only because it assumes saved scans never change.
A ties each page token to a saved record version and refuses it after a change. C ties continuations to the chosen values only. B has no clear paging step.
C gives each view its own request and error state. A puts every view in one read action. B builds every view in one handler but splits the building work into separate parts.
B stores the choice in the URL so it can be reloaded or shared. A and C keep the choice only in browser memory.
Each needs different parent designs: A only d734, B f0c461 and 877208, C all three.
limitations: All three keep the same core: the browser owns the choice, every request names its inputs, the browser checks each reply, and saved scans are only read. The variety is in details, not in that core.
A and C differ mostly in how they split up views and handle failures. They are close to the same design.
Different numbers of parts do not mean different behavior. B's many parts carry out the same reply check as A and C.
unexplored_directions: Build views ahead of time when a scan is saved, instead of building them when a user asks.
Give each item an ID that stays the same across scans, so history can match items reliably.
Store history differences when a scan is saved, instead of computing them when a user asks.
Have the server send updates when a new scan finishes, instead of waiting for the browser to ask.
Return one combined reply covering all views for a choice, so every view shows the same moment in time.

evidence: The scope requires graph pages to stay tied to the chosen saved scan and query.
The scope forbids old replies from replacing browser results for a newer choice.
The scope says discovery of every runtime relationship is not guaranteed.
A's page tokens include the saved record version and are refused after a change.
B assumes saved scans never change and keys its cache on scan ID, query fingerprint, view kind and builder version.
B lists its compatibility with parent d734 as unknown.
C keeps a separate loading and error state for each view and claims to work with all three parents.
No source code was supplied. All three alternatives are proposals only.
value_json.summary: All three designs share the same core. The browser holds the user's current choice. Every request names the scan and query. The browser throws away any reply that no longer matches the current choice. They differ in three ways. First, how much server work is split into parts and whether built pages are kept for reuse. Second, what each assumes about saved scans changing after they are written. Third, which parent design each can work with. A and C are close: no stored pages, reads go through the parent, and they differ mainly in how failures are kept apart. B splits the server work into many small parts, keeps built pages for reuse (a cache), and depends on saved scans never changing. None of the three says how history matches the same item across two scans.
unknowns: How history views tell newer interpretations apart. The scope lists this as open.
Whether saved scans store an analysis rules version, stable record versions and source excerpts.
Query syntax, graph order, page size limits and how long records are kept.
How history matches the same item across two scans.
What happens when a scan is deleted while someone is paging or comparing it.
Workload sizes that would show whether a cache or parallel paging is needed.

value_json.summary: The assessment is sound and I approve it. It recommends no change. Remote job handling is the one place where actors (independent owners that change their own private state only when they receive messages) could fit. The supplied code already protects jobs in other ways. Each job has a time-limited ownership claim called a lease. A token check on the server rejects stale owners. A cancellable renewal task keeps leases alive, and tests cover long calls, expired leases and temporary failures. The assessment cites real lines, compares smaller options such as a single job record, and lists risks and checks to keep. The issues below are small and do not change the result.

supporting_evidence_json: Scope s09 takes findings about repository parts and returns accounts of responsibilities and design that those findings support.
Dependency s08 provides saved scan results and progress information. It does not run or change studied source.
Product s01 requires results to keep evidence, uncertainty, and input freshness, and to disclose anything shortened.
All three parent alternatives for s05 leave saving and access to the parent, or to the parent's claim book, and need evidence-linked responsibility claims.

cons: Seven steps add more code to hand data between steps than a single writer would.
Requiring a statement tag on every sentence can make the writing stiff. It can also drop useful connecting sentences.
Returning the full statement list makes results larger.
The checker confirms that sentences link to statements. It cannot confirm that a sentence says the same thing as the statement it links to.

assumptions: Findings from s08 carry stable IDs that statements can link to.
The parent supplies freshness information and the selected scan and query.
Statement lists are small enough to return in full with each result.
boundary_rules: Wording can rephrase statements but cannot create facts.
Every sentence a reader sees links to a statement, and every statement links to findings.
Guesses, observations, and suggestions stay labeled separately all the way to the output.
This capability never writes to saved scans, saved results, or repository files.
Repository text is quoted evidence and is never followed as an instruction.

contracts: Rejects a set of findings that comes from more than one scan, and says why.
Never reads repository files. Treats source text and comments only as quoted evidence.
Copies the fact that the parent's freshness note is present onto the bundle, but does not change the note.
components.name: Findings intake
components.responsibility: Receives findings for one selected saved scan and query. Freezes them as a read-only bundle. Computes a short identifying code from the scan, the query, the settings, and the method version. Equal inputs always give an equal code.

contracts: Every item keeps its evidence links.
A guess is never moved into the directly-seen pile.
A missing relationship goes into the cannot-answer pile. It is not treated as proof that the parts are unrelated.
components.name: Fact sorter
components.responsibility: Splits the bundle into three piles: things the scan saw directly, guesses about what a group of parts is for, and questions the findings cannot answer.

contracts: Each statement makes exactly one point.
When two pieces of evidence disagree, both statements are kept and the disagreement is marked.
A number such as a score is stored with a sentence that says what it counted and what it cannot show.
components.name: Statement builder
components.responsibility: Turns sorted facts into statements of the form 'part, action, other part or job'. Each statement gets an ID, evidence links, and a level of certainty with a reason.

contracts: Every statement left out because of size is listed, with a count.
A review judgment must name the statements it relies on and the rule it judges by.
Suggested changes are labeled as suggestions, with their expected benefit and cost.
components.name: Account planner
components.responsibility: Chooses which statements appear in each requested account (an explanation, a responsibility map, or a design review), and in what order. Applies any size limit the caller gives.

contracts: May reorder, join, or simplify statements. May not add a new fact, a new relationship, or more certainty than the statement has.
Keeps the words that show uncertainty, such as 'appears to' or 'not known'.
components.name: Wording writer
components.responsibility: Writes short, plain sentences or JSON entries for the planned statements. Tags each sentence with the IDs of the statements it expresses.

contracts: A removed sentence makes the account 'partly checked', and the account says so.
Does not edit sentences. It only keeps or removes them.
components.name: Trace checker
components.responsibility: Compares the written account with the plan. Removes any sentence that has no statement tag, or whose tag is not in the plan. Records each removal.

contracts: Each account has its own state: complete, partly checked, stopped early, or failed.
Returns all the data in full, so the parent can save it or shorten it for delivery and say what it left out.
components.name: Result packager
components.responsibility: Puts together the accounts, the statement list, the omission list, the identifying code, and a completion state for each account. Hands the result to the parent.

design.control_model: The parent makes one call with findings, the requested account kinds, settings, an optional size limit, and a cancellation signal. The steps run in order: intake, sort, statements, plan, then wording and checking once for each requested account. Before each step, the run checks whether it has been cancelled. If a frozen statement list from an earlier run with the same identifying code is supplied, the run skips straight to planning. No queue, background job, or separate service is added.
extension_strategy: Add a new account kind by adding a planning rule. The statement list stays the same.
Add a new review rule as a planner rule that names the statements it needs.
Swap the wording writer, for example a fixed template versus an AI model, without changing earlier steps. The checker stays the same.
design.failure_isolation: If intake fails, no account is produced, and the parent receives a clear reason. If wording fails for one account kind, the other kinds are still returned. The statement list is still returned, so wording can be retried without rebuilding it. If checking removes sentences, only those sentences are lost. A cancelled run returns finished accounts and marks the rest as stopped early. A crash of the whole process loses unsaved work. Protection against that comes from the parent.
information_flows: In: findings tied to one scan and query, requested account kinds, settings, size limit, and the parent's freshness note.
Inside: frozen bundle, then sorted piles, then statement list with evidence links and certainty, then a plan for each account, then tagged sentences.
Out: accounts with a state for each one, the statement list, the omission list, the sentence-removal notes, and the identifying code.

design.summary: Turn findings into accounts in two separate stages. In the first stage, findings become a plain list of statements. Each statement says one thing, such as 'part A sends work to part B'. It also lists its evidence links and how sure it is. In the second stage, the statements become readable sentences. The wording stage may only rephrase statements from the list. It cannot add new facts. A checker then confirms that every sentence points back to at least one statement. Each stage hands the next one a finished, unchangeable copy of its result. Accounts are returned together with their statement list, and this capability saves nothing itself. The parent can store the list, or it can be rebuilt later from the same inputs.

assessments.change_isolation: A new analysis kind only needs a new assignment kind, under the same acceptance rules. Changing the start rules touches the owner, which also holds the other run logic. Those changes are less contained than in B, where start rules live in their own component.
assessments.control_flow: The owner sends work to workers. It checks the start, asks for the source, saves each assignment before sending it, checks each reply against the saved assignment, and finishes the run when every assignment has an outcome. Progress is counted from saved assignment states.
assessments.data_ownership: The owner controls run states, assignments, accepted findings, and completion decisions. These records are edited in place in the application's shared store. Workers keep only temporary data. Finished scans never change, and a rerun gets a new ID.
assessments.decomposition: There are three parts. The scan owner holds all run logic. The source reader reads files and keeps them. Workers analyze the copied text. Planning, accepting replies, and building the final scan all sit inside the owner.
assessments.failure_isolation: A failed worker affects only its own assignment. If saving fails, the owner stops taking results and sending work. After a restart it picks up from the saved assignments and may repeat unfinished work. If the shared application or store is lost, every run stops.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers every required input and output: reading allowed source, saved settings, start requests, worker replies, saved scans, and progress. It keeps captured source, so evidence still works after the files change. It saves incomplete scans with their gaps listed, which supports looking at history and what was missed.
assessments.justified_complexity: There are only three parts and no extra service. Direct calls inside the existing application keep it small. The cost is that atomic updates and run claims must come from the shared store. The proposal admits that support for them is unverified.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs inside the existing application and uses its workers. Captured source needs a rule for how long it is kept. Testing covers duplicate replies, late replies, interrupted saves, denied starts, and files that change during capture.
strengths: One owner decides starts, accepts replies, and saves results. Accepted findings and reported progress come from the same saved records, so they cannot disagree.
It accepts a reply only for the active attempt, checked by run, work item, and attempt number. Duplicate and late replies are rejected.
Partial or interrupted scans are still saved, and clearly marked incomplete. This fits the product rule that omissions must be disclosed.
It is the only design that returns a reason without starting when the start check cannot decide.
weaknesses: The owner holds many jobs: start checks, retries, saving, and completion. A mistake there affects every step.

It needs atomic writes, meaning a result and its work status are saved together or not at all. It also needs an exclusive claim on each run. The proposal itself says the shared store may not support these.
It says little about retry limits and cancellation.
It assumes only one parent design (83ec). That limits which parents it can be combined with.

assessments.change_isolation: This design is the best at keeping changes local. Start rules live only in the start check. A new AI task kind adds one planner rule and one answer-shape check. The event list and the scan builder stay the same.
assessments.control_flow: Workers ask for tasks. Claims expire on a timer and are noticed when the list is next read, so no background timer is needed. The reply check tells the builder after each task finishes, and the builder seals the scan when all tasks are done.
assessments.data_ownership: The event list is the only owner of work state, and its entries are never edited while a scan is open. The snapshot store holds the copied file text, which never changes. The parent owns settings, access rules, and sealed scans. Nothing else keeps a second copy of progress.
assessments.decomposition: Each job is its own component: start check, snapshot, structure reader, planner, event list, handout, reply check, scan builder, and progress counter. Only the event list and the snapshot store keep state.
assessments.failure_isolation: A worker that hangs lets its claim expire. The task is retried up to a limit, then marked failed. Bad or late answers are rejected and the reason is recorded. Building the scan again after a crash gives the same result. Losing the event list or the snapshot store stops all scans.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers all required inputs and outputs. Each saved scan records the snapshot hash, settings version, rules version, completion state, and missing items. That supports history and disclosed omissions. Progress gives detailed counts. It cannot show results before sealing.
assessments.justified_complexity: Splitting the work into many single-job steps that keep nothing between calls makes each step easy to check and safe to repeat. Whether the event list and the replaying are worth their cost depends on scan size and how much crash recovery matters. Neither is measured in the payload.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs inside the parent's local service. Workers can be separate processes that ask for work. Snapshot storage must be affordable. Claim time limits and retry limits are not given. Slow polling by workers adds delay.
strengths: All work state lives in one list of events that is only added to. Replaying that list after a crash rebuilds every scan, and no accepted work is lost.
Each task ID is a hash of its inputs. A hash is a short code computed from content. So two start requests for the same repository state create one scan, and repeating an answer has no extra effect.
A separate step reads structure and relationships from the copied text with no AI. Its output is repeatable and marked as either read directly or guessed.
It is the only design with explicit cancellation. Cancelling adds one event, and the scan is then saved as incomplete.
It claims to fit all three parent designs. Two of those claims are marked unverified.
weaknesses: It has nine parts, the most of any design. More parts means more to build and test.
Progress is recounted by replaying events every time someone asks. This may get slow on large scans unless old events are compressed.
Nothing is visible until the scan is sealed, so early inspection is not possible.
Only one worker may hold a task at a time. That needs a safe 'claim if still free' step on the event list. The design does not say how two claims arriving at once are prevented.
Its worker contract does not say that source text and comments must be treated as data, not instructions. A and C both say this.

assessments.change_isolation: New task kinds need a clear list of inputs and outputs. Publishing partial scans is deferred until rules for labeling them exist. Changing the start rules touches the controller, which also runs the rest of each run.
assessments.control_flow: The controller sends each task with an expiry time and an attempt number. Replies count only after they pass checks and are saved. Expired attempts are replaced within a retry limit. When every required task has succeeded, the controller asks the writer to publish. Otherwise the run ends as failed.
assessments.data_ownership: The parent's record store holds all lasting data. Run records can change and keep accepted outputs. Published scans never change. The controller keeps only temporary state. The saved copy of the source stays with its run until retention rules allow removal.
assessments.decomposition: There are five parts. The controller moves runs forward. The records part owns runs, attempts, and published scans. The source reader also plans tasks. Workers analyze. The scan writer builds the published scan.
assessments.failure_isolation: A failed worker affects only its own task, and late replies cannot overwrite a newer attempt. A failed save leaves the run waiting for another try, and no half-saved scan appears complete. A storage failure stops progress for every run.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers source reading, saved settings, start requests, worker replies, saved scans, and progress. Partial results are not available to inspect when a required task fails. The rules version is saved when known and marked unknown otherwise.
assessments.justified_complexity: It has five parts. The separate scan writer and record owner add some structure beyond A. In return, unfinished work stays apart from published scans. The proposal says conditional updates and retries add coordination work.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs inside the existing application, with no queue service. The record store must support conditional updates and a single step that makes a scan visible. Retention, task size, and retry limits are unspecified.
strengths: Unfinished run records are kept apart from published scans. Readers only see scans that were fully saved.
A conditional update applies only if the record has not changed since it was read. This stops two controller attempts from moving the same run forward twice.
Retries use the saved copy of the files, never the current ones. It reports files that changed during reading instead of claiming one consistent version.
Progress includes the time of the last saved update. It does not claim that a silent worker is still making progress.
weaknesses: If a required task fails, no scan is published. The accepted work stays only in the run record and cannot be browsed as a scan. That clashes with the product rule to keep and disclose partial results.
Task records also act as the work queue. That adds task selection and expiry checks inside the application.
It assumes only one parent design (b5ee).
It does not say whether it can start a separate process for each worker.

composition_conflicts: The designs need different parent designs. A needs parent 83ec. C needs parent b5ee. B claims to fit all three, but two of those claims are unverified.
Mixing B's event list with the editable run records of A or C would give work state two owners. Their progress counts could then disagree.
C's rule of publishing nothing on failure conflicts with A and B, which save incomplete scans. Parent readers would see different scan sets depending on the design chosen.
disagreements: Partial results: A and B save incomplete scans that people can inspect. C publishes only when every required task succeeds.
Where state lives: B treats its event list as the only record of truth and recomputes progress from it. A and C treat the current record as the truth.
How many parts are needed: B splits planning, structure reading, the work handout, reply checks, and scan building into separate parts. A keeps almost all of that inside one owner.

differences: How work state is stored: A and C edit saved records in place. B only adds events to a list and works out the current state by replaying them.
How work reaches workers: A and C send tasks out. B waits for workers to ask.
When some work fails: A and B save the scan marked incomplete, with the gaps listed. C publishes nothing and marks the run failed.
Repeated start requests: B returns the existing scan for the same files and settings. C uses an ID supplied by the caller. A gives every start a new run ID.
B alone has a structure-reading step that uses no AI, and an explicit way to cancel a scan.
limitations: A and C differ mostly in how they handle failure and in how many parts they split the work into. Their basic shape is the same: one manager edits saved task records and sends tasks to workers.
No design was checked against real code or real storage guarantees.
unexplored_directions: Scans that only redo the files whose content hash changed since an earlier saved scan.
Showing accepted results while a scan is still running, labeled as unfinished.
Running workers in separate processes, so one crash cannot take down every run.
Limits on how many runs can happen at once, and cooldown rules for start requests.

value_json.summary: All three designs read the repository without running it. They save a copy of the files they studied, hand work to AI workers, check each worker reply before counting it, and save a final scan that never changes. A and C are close. In both, one manager edits saved work records in place, sends tasks to workers, and counts progress from those records. They differ mainly in what happens when some work fails. A saves the scan and marks it incomplete. C saves no scan and marks the run failed. B works differently. It keeps all work state in a list of events that is only ever added to. Workers ask for tasks instead of being sent them. Task IDs are built from the task's inputs, so asking to start the same scan twice does no harm. B also has a separate step that reads code structure from text alone, with no AI. All three depend on one shared store. All three leave the start rules undefined. All three are kept.

Whether the shared store supports atomic writes, conditional updates, or a safe 'claim if still free' step.

issues.explanation: The assessment does not cite the clearest sign that history-import state must survive a restart. history_jobs.py sets CLAIM_STALE_SECONDS to 300. It also has _pid_is_running, which asks the operating system whether a process ID is still alive. Together these show the code expects a worker process to die and its claim to be taken over later. semantic_leases.py also sets a 30-second heartbeat interval, a regular 'still working' signal that keeps a lease alive.

issues.explanation: The conformance score (how much of the pattern the code already uses) is 65. That is slightly generous. The assessment itself says safe handling of repeated, late, or reordered results is not shown. The card's main safety rule depends on that handling. Something in the high 50s would match the stated gap better. The number is a judgment, not a measurement, and the recommendation does not depend on it.

issues.explanation: The detector picked these files because each made two or more connect() calls. It treated those calls as 'registrations'. Four of the eight files are tests, and one is a benchmark script. The assessment rightly rejects connect() calls as proof of coordination. It still lists the four test files as affected targets. Readers could mistake them for places to change, when they are only places to check the work.

value_json.summary: I approve the assessment. It says to keep the current saved job controls, and that fits the evidence. A process manager is code that saves a long task's progress and decides the next step after each message or failure. History imports, leased analysis jobs, and graph-cache rebuilding each have their own version of this, inside their own service. The assessment correctly rejects the detector's matches as weak evidence. Those matches were plain database.connect() calls, not real registrations. value_json.detail: Builds an ordered list of repository checks, smoke runs, and an optional benchmark, then executes them from the repository root. Unless skipped, browser checks install npm dependencies, create a temporary fixture repository and database, launch a local server, wait for its health endpoint, run visual tests on the host or in a container, and stop the server. The command-line entry point returns 0 after the gate completes; subprocess failures propagate.
evidence: Module docstring: runs the complete local AnaxiGraph quality gate in CI-equivalent order.
Function bodies define command ordering, temporary output paths, browser server lifecycle, parser options, and success status.

functions.overview: Prints and executes a command from the given root, raising on a nonzero exit.
Builds ordered quality-check commands and includes the baseline benchmark unless it is skipped.
Installs npm dependencies, starts a temporary fixture server, runs visual browser tests with the selected runner, and stops the server.
Starts the fixture server with repository, database, host, port, and scan-on-start arguments, logging its output.
Polls the server health endpoint up to 120 times and raises with the log contents if the server exits or never becomes ready.
Returns a locally allocated loopback port.
Constructs a Docker command to run visual tests against the local server.
Terminates the server, escalating to kill if it does not stop within the timeout.
Defines CLI options for the coverage base, browser runner, and skipping browser or benchmark checks.
Parses options, runs quality commands and optional browser contracts, then prints success and returns 0.

value_json.overview: Runs the AnaxiGraph quality gate and optional browser contracts in CI-equivalent order.

The runner reads evidence once, builds a map if needed, and runs each requested written output in sequence. A failed output does not prevent another independent output from running.
